questions.stem: A passage about a nineteenth-century reading of a medieval assembly says: "A nineteenth-century reading highlights representation but may overstate modern parallels" Drawing on that evidence, note 2156 asks how to correct the reading.

options.text: Nineteenth-century historians read medieval assemblies as modern parliaments.
A medieval assembly had no representative function at all.
Nineteenth-century views were entirely objective.
options.misconception: reads the evidence as Nineteenth-century views were entirely objective instead of A nineteenth-century reading highlights representation but may….

options.text: A nineteenth-century reading highlights representation but may overstate modern parallels.

questions.explanation: A nineteenth-century reading can highlight representation but may overstate modern parallels. The error is to treat it as objective or to deny consultation.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: 1914 and 1945 read as a pair
questions.learningObjective: Compare 1914 and 1945 as a paired marker

stimulus.body: Source note: 1914 opens the crisis and 1945 closes its second phase, so the pair frames one long conflict. This is the claim the evidence in the topic supports.

questions.stem: The class reading on 1914 and 1945 read as a pair records: "1914 opens the crisis and 1945 closes its second phase, so the pair frames one long conflict" Taking that statement as given, note 2157 asks how a translator should render the pair's meaning.

options.text: 1914 opens the crisis and 1945 closes its second phase, so the pair frames one long conflict.
1914 and 1945 are interchangeable labels for the same war.
1945 makes 1914 irrelevant to European order.
Only 1914 matters because it started everything.
options.misconception: reads the evidence as Only 1914 matters because it started everything instead of 1914 opens the crisis and 1945 closes its second phase, so the….

questions.explanation: 1914 and 1945 work as a pair because the first opens the crisis and the second closes its second phase. The error is to collapse them into one war or to discard the earlier date.
questions.hint: Pair the opening and closing dates.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Ordering a causal chain of institutions
questions.learningObjective: Order a causal chain of institutions

stimulus.body: Source note: Ordering a causal chain of institutions. A causal chain must be ordered so each institution precedes and enables the next; reversing or randomising the sequence breaks the argument.

questions.stem: With reference to the source note, explain order a causal chain of institutions.

answer.exemplar: A causal chain must be ordered so each institution precedes and enables the next; reversing or randomising the sequence breaks the argument.

questions.explanation: A causal chain of institutions must run in chronological order, with each step enabling the next. The error is to reverse or randomise the sequence.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Counting a long course
questions.learningObjective: Count a long historical course phase by phase

stimulus.body: A translator's note counts a long course. It asks if rounding distorts a long course. The note stresses that phases between markers matter.

questions.stem: The source text on counting a long course states: "A long course is counted phase by phase, not just by endpoints" Working from that claim, note 2159 checks if rounding distorts a long course.

options.text: A long course can be counted by its endpoints alone.
options.misconception: confuses A long course can be counted by its endpoints alone with the supported claim A long course is counted phase by phase, not just by endpoints.

options.text: Counting a course means averaging its start and end dates.
A long course is counted phase by phase, not just by endpoints.
The duration equals the number of institutions involved.

questions.explanation: A long course is counted phase by phase rather than by endpoints alone. The error is to reduce a process to its first and last dates.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a bare chronology can establish
questions.learningObjective: State what a bare chronology can establish

stimulus.body: Source note: A bare chronology establishes order and duration, not causes or meanings. This is the claim the evidence in the topic supports.

questions.stem: The source text on what a bare chronology can establish states: "A bare chronology establishes order and duration, not causes or meanings" Working from that claim, note 2160 checks if chronology needs interpretation.

options.text: A bare chronology proves why events happened.
A list of dates can settle moral responsibility.
Chronology alone shows how people felt.
A bare chronology establishes order and duration, not causes or meanings.

questions.explanation: A bare chronology gives order and duration but not causes or meanings. The error is to treat dates as explanations.
